traveler: Margery Kempe (Margery Brunham of Bishop's Lynn)
title: The Weeping Pilgrim of Lynn: the Brewhouse, the Roaring at Calvary, and the Book Lost Five Hundred Years
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: King's Lynn Minster, the merchant's daughter at the font
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the year is back-calculated from her own statement of her age at marriage, and no baptismal record survives
stops.campa: Bishop's Lynn stands where the Great Ouse runs out to the Wash, and its wool quays and Hanse warehouses make merchants rich. John Brunham is one of them, five times mayor of the town, and his daughter is carried to the font of St Margaret's among the best families of the borough. She will live her whole life within a mile of this church and be known for it from Norfolk to the Holy Sepulchre. Nothing at the christening marks her out. She is a burgess's child in a prosperous port, and Lynn expects of her what it expects of the rest.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: St Margaret's, now King's Lynn Minster, parish church of her baptism and her marriage

stops.name: King's Lynn Minster, married to John Kempe
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Book's own statement of her age; the calendar year is the standard scholarly placement
stops.campa: At twenty or a little more she is married to John Kempe, a burgess of the town, in the church where she was christened. It is the match Lynn makes for its own: a merchant's daughter to a man of the guilds, who will hold town office the year after the wedding. What the office was, no record reachable now will say. She is with child within a short time. At least fourteen children will follow, and the book of her life will name almost none of them, keeping instead the memory of the first, and of what the first one cost her.
stops.quote: Whan this creatur was twenty yer of age or sumdele mor, sche was maryed to a worschepful burgeys and was wyth chylde wythin schort tyme.
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 1 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 1
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The burgess registers of Bishop's Lynn for 1394, which record John Kempe in town office without naming it

stops.name: Kempe household, the devils and the man in the purple mantle
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Book dates the crisis only by its length, half a year, eight weeks and odd days
stops.campa: The first childbirth nearly kills her, and a confessor cuts her off sharply before she can confess the sin she has carried for years. What follows lasts half a year, eight weeks and odd days: devils with open mouths, hands that tear her own skin, servants who must bind her. Then a man sits down on the side of her bed, clad in a mantle of purple silk, and asks why she has forsaken him when he never forsook her. He rises into the air so slowly she can watch him go. She is in her right mind again from that hour, and asks for the keys of the buttery.
stops.quote: sche dyspered of hyr lyfe ... this creatur went owt of hir minde and was wondyrlye vexid and labowryd wyth spyritys half yer eight wekys and odde days.
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 1 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 1
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The Proem and first chapter of the Book, the earliest first-person account of postpartum derangement in English

stops.name: Tuesday Market Place, one of the greatest brewers in the town
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Book gives no year, and this placement sits editorially between the marriage and the devotional turn
stops.campa: She wants a trade of her own, and money of her own, and the fine hoods of gold pipes that turn heads at Mass. So she brews. For three or four years she is one of the greatest brewers in Lynn, and then the ale begins to fail: the barm stands fair on the surface as any man could wish, and then falls, and the whole brewing is lost, batch after batch, until her servants are ashamed and will not stay with her. She loses much goods. She had never been trained to it, and she says so plainly.
stops.quote: sche gan to brewyn and was on of the grettest brewers in the town N a three yer or four tyl sche lost mech good
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 2 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition); the edition prints 'the town N', the manuscript's abbreviation for Lynn
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 2
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The brewing trade of late fourteenth-century Lynn, one of the few crafts open to a married woman on her own account

stops.name: Tuesday Market Place, the horse that would not draw
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Book places the mill immediately after the brewery without giving a year
stops.campa: Ale having failed her, she buys a horse-mill and two good horses and hires a man to grind corn for the town. The first horse will not draw. Whatever the man does, it goes backward rather than forward, and when he unyokes it, it eats well enough. The second horse does the same. The man leaves. The story runs through Lynn that God is against her, and she agrees: she reads the ale and the horses together as one judgment on her pride, and turns from the trade of the town toward the life that will make her notorious in it.
stops.quote: this hors wold drawe no drawt in the mylle for nothing the man mygth do ... he wold rather gon bakward than forward
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 2 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 2
suggested_refs: Horse-mills of the Norfolk market towns, the second of her two failed ventures

stops.name: King's Lynn Minster, the melody and the beginning of tears
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no consulted source fixes a year for the melody, and the loud crying itself does not begin until Jerusalem in 1414
stops.campa: Lying in bed beside her husband she hears a melody so sweet that she starts up and says that it is full merry in heaven. From that night she cannot hear mirth or worldly song without weeping, and at the sacring of the Mass the tears come whether she wills them or not. She wears the hair cloth under her gown where no one sees it, goes to confession two and three times a day, and asks her husband for the thing he will not yet grant her. The town, which knew her as a brewer, begins to watch her at her prayers.
stops.quote: Alas, that evyr I dede synne, it is ful mery in hevyn.
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 3 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 3
suggested_refs: The chapters of heavenly melody, the hair cloth, and the beginning of her weeping at the sacring

stops.name: The road between York and Bridlington, the vow of chastity
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Book places the scene on Midsummer Eve without naming the exact spot on the road
stops.campa: It is a hot Friday on the Yorkshire road, and John Kempe carries a bottle of beer and a cake in his bosom. He asks her what she would do if a man came with a sword to strike off his head unless he lay with her again: would she suffer him killed, or suffer his body. She says she would rather see him slain. He tells her she is no good wife. Then they strike the bargain that has been years in coming. She will pay his debts before she goes to Jerusalem; she will eat and drink with him on Fridays; he will not come into her bed again.
stops.quote: Grawntyth me that ye schal not komyn in my bed, and I grawnt yow to qwyte yowr dettys ... makyth my body fre to God ... I schal etyn and drynkyn on the Fryday at yowr byddyng
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 11 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 11
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The wayside cross on the Bridlington road where the vow was sealed over bread and beer

stops.name: Lincoln, before Philip Repyngdon
stops.date_confidence: attested as belonging to 1413, before the Jerusalem journey; Repyngdon holds Lincoln from 1405 to 1419
stops.campa: She and John Kempe come before the Bishop of Lincoln to have the vow of chastity made formal and the mantle and ring of a vowess granted to her. Repyngdon receives them kindly, hears her, and gives her the vow. On the white clothing he will not act: she is of his diocese in body but the clothing is a matter for Canterbury, and he sends her on to the archbishop. Bishops will handle her this way for the next twenty years, finding nothing against her and passing her upward to someone with more authority to be troubled by it.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I chs. 15-16
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The episcopal register of Philip Repyngdon, Bishop of Lincoln 1405-1419

stops.name: Lambeth, before Archbishop Thomas Arundel
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1413 by necessity: Arundel dies on 19 February 1414, which rules out the later dating sometimes given
stops.campa: In the archbishop's garden at Lambeth she talks with Thomas Arundel until the stars come out. He is the man whose constitutions have made unlicensed preaching and English scripture into hanging matters, and she has come to ask his leave to choose her own confessor and to wear white. He grants both. Before that she rebukes his household to their faces for swearing and for their loose talk, in his own hall, and he does not stop her. She leaves with the letter she came for, granted by the man who wrote those constitutions.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 16
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: Arundel's Constitutions of 1409, the legal frame under which Kempe's speech was repeatedly tested

stops.name: St Julian's Church, Norwich, the anchoress weighs the tears
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period before the Jerusalem journey; the Book gives no month
stops.campa: She goes to the anchoress walled into the little church of St Julian to have her visions weighed by someone who will not flatter her. They talk for days. Julian tells her to measure every revelation by whether it moves toward charity, that the Holy Ghost never urges anything against the worship of God, and that tears such as hers are the token of his presence and not of madness. Two women in a cell the width of a room settle what the bishops of England will spend the next twenty years reopening.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 18
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The anchorhold at St Julian's, Norwich, demolished in the 1530s; the present cell is a 1950s reconstruction

stops.name: Great Yarmouth, taking ship for the Low Countries
stops.date_confidence: attested as the point of departure; the Book gives no sailing date
stops.campa: John Kempe brings her as far as the Norfolk coast and turns back. She takes ship at Yarmouth with a company of English pilgrims bound for the Holy Land by way of Zeeland, the Rhine and the Alps, carrying almost nothing and paying her way as she goes. She is about forty, mother of fourteen, lately a brewer, and she is going to Jerusalem. The company is polite on the quay. Within weeks they will be trying to be rid of her, and they will keep trying at every stage of the road for the next two years.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 26
suggested_refs: St Nicholas, Great Yarmouth, the great parish church of the port from which she sailed

stops.name: Zierikzee, the sackcloth apron
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Book gives no month
stops.campa: In Zeeland the weeping begins in earnest at table and at Mass, and her companions cannot bear it. They will not have her eat with them. They cut up a piece of white canvas and make her wear it as an apron, so that she will be taken for a fool and no one will think she belongs to them. She wears it. They take her money for their keeping and give her back less than she gave, and she goes on with them anyway, because the road to Jerusalem does not run through any country where a woman travels alone.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 26
suggested_refs: The white canvas apron of Zierikzee, the first of the marks put on her by her own countrymen

stops.name: Constance, the legate takes her side
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Book gives no month, and the visit precedes the great council held in the same city from 1414
stops.campa: At Constance the English company lays its case before a papal legate lodged in the city: this woman weeps, will not eat meat, speaks of the Gospel at meals, and shames them wherever they go. The legate hears them and then hears her. He will not command her to eat meat, he will not forbid her tears, and he lets her keep her own confessor. Her countrymen are told they must bear with her. They abandon her in the city instead, and she goes on to Bologna with an old man named William Weaver who is afraid of the roads.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 27
suggested_refs: The papal legate's judgment at Constance, the first formal clerical ruling in her favour

stops.name: Bologna, taken back on condition of silence
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Book names Bologna outright, contrary to route reconstructions that treat it as inference
stops.campa: She reaches Bologna before her old company does, which they had not thought possible. When they arrive they offer her terms: she may travel with them again if she will not speak of the Gospel where they are, and will sit still at meals as they bid her, and will make merry with them at supper. She agrees to all of it. She keeps the bargain the length of Lombardy, silent at table among people who have measured her worth exactly, and rides into Venice with them as one of the company.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 27
suggested_refs: The Bologna agreement, the terms on which her fellow pilgrims would tolerate her

stops.name: Venice, thirteen weeks waiting for a galley
stops.date_confidence: attested as about thirteen weeks across the winter of 1413 to 1414; the Book gives no month
stops.campa: Thirteen weeks in Venice, waiting for a ship. She receives communion every Sunday with great weeping and violent sobbing, and the company breaks its bargain and turns on her again, at table, in the street, aboard the galley they finally hire. They will not let her sit at meat with them; they cut her gown short and make her wear a white canvas smock again so she is taken for a fool. She buys bedding for the voyage, and finds when she goes aboard that they have taken her sheets. She sails with them regardless.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 28
suggested_refs: The Venetian pilgrim galleys, the regulated passenger trade that carried Latin Christendom to Jaffa

stops.name: Jaffa, the landing on the Palestinian shore
stops.date_confidence: attested as the point of disembarkation; the Book gives no date
stops.campa: The galley puts its pilgrims ashore at Jaffa, the port that has served this traffic since the treaty of 1192 opened the holy places to unarmed Christians, and the party is counted, taxed, and assigned to the Franciscan guides who will take it inland by donkey. Her companions have told the friars in advance what she is. She is so weak in body that she has to be helped onto the ass. Two hundred and forty miles of Lombardy and the sea are behind her and the city she has crossed Christendom to see is a day and a half away.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 28
suggested_refs: The Franciscan custody of the Holy Land, which licensed and guided every Western pilgrim party of the period

stops.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the crying begins
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Book gives no calendar date, and the friars kept the party in the church overnight
stops.campa: The friars carry lights and lead the pilgrims from station to station inside the church, telling at each what Christ suffered there. At the place of the Crucifixion she sees it happening in front of her, and the cry comes out of her for the first time: not weeping now but roaring, so that she cannot stand or hold herself up, and spreads her arms wide and turns her body about. It will come on her fourteen times in a day for years afterward, in Rome, in Leicester, in Lynn. She takes for her pattern the Magdalene, who wept at this same tomb and was not shamed for it.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 28
suggested_refs: The chapel of Calvary within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where the gift of tears is said to begin

stops.name: Mount of Olives, held up on either side
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Book gives no date within the three weeks in the Holy Land
stops.campa: From the slope of the Mount of Olives the whole city lies open across the valley, and she looks at it and thinks of what was done in it. She weeps so hard she cannot stand alone, and two pilgrims hold her up under the arms, one on either side, until it passes. Then she asks to be shown where the Lord's feet stood when he ascended, and where his mother wept. The friars take the party on. Twenty years later, in Lynn, she has the day set down by a priest writing at her dictation.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 28
suggested_refs: The Mount of Olives station of the Franciscan pilgrim circuit

stops.name: Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Book gives no date
stops.campa: In the grotto beneath the great basilica the pilgrims are shown the place of the birth and the manger, and she is taken again with the loud crying in front of them all. Her visions have run to the Nativity for years in Lynn, and she has been at the birth in her own mind many times: warming the child, begging swaddling bands from good wives, following the mother into Egypt. Now the rock itself is under her hands. She weeps here as she wept at the sepulchre, and her companions endure it as they have learned to.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 29
suggested_refs: The Grotto of the Nativity beneath the Constantinian basilica at Bethlehem

stops.name: Qasr el Yahud, the Jordan and the wilderness beyond
stops.date_confidence: attested that she made the extended circuit; the exact bank is not named, and the pin follows the customary pilgrim baptism site
stops.campa: The extended tour costs extra, and she pays it: down through the Judaean hills to the river where Christ was baptised, and on to the mountain of the forty days where the fasting and the temptation were, and to Bethany where Lazarus came out of the tomb. The heat is severe and she is not strong. Her companions will not wait for her on the mountain and she climbs it with two Saracens hired to help her, one under each arm, which she counts a kindness. She is in the Holy Land three weeks in all.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 29
suggested_refs: The Jordan baptism site and the Mount of Temptation, the paid extension of the standard circuit

stops.name: Assisi, the Lammas Day pardon
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Book names Assisi and the Lammas Day indulgence, though the year is fixed only by the shape of the return journey
stops.campa: She turns aside on the road from Venice to Rome for the pardon granted at Assisi on the first of August, the indulgence Francis begged for the little church he rebuilt with his own hands, and stands in the crowd of pilgrims come for it from every country. Here she is taken up by Dame Margaret Florentyne, a great lady of Rome travelling with the Knights of Rhodes, who puts her in her own company and brings her the rest of the way south. She has come from Jerusalem with nothing, and she arrives in Rome as a rich woman's guest.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 31
suggested_refs: The Portiuncula indulgence of 1 August, and the church of San Francesco raised over the saint's tomb

stops.name: Hospital of St Thomas of Canterbury, Rome, put out of the house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Roman stay, which runs from autumn 1414 until she leaves at Easter 1415; the month here is a placement
stops.campa: At the English hospice she is at first well received, and then an English priest who cannot endure her crying turns the house against her and she is put out of it. She gives away everything she has, borrows nothing, and begs her bread in the streets of Rome through the winter, serving an old woman for six weeks and carrying her water and sticks. In the end the same priest tests her, is satisfied, and the hospice takes her back. She receives the white clothes again here, and the ring, and is married to the Godhead at the Apostles.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I chs. 31-33
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The English hospice of St Thomas on the Via di Monserrato, ancestor of the Venerable English College

stops.name: Middelburg, the crossing home
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no month, and she leaves Rome at Easter 1415
stops.campa: She comes north out of Italy through the Alps in company she does not choose, sick, penniless, and taken for a fool by most of those she travels with. At Middelburg in Zeeland she receives the sacrament and waits for a passage. The sea crossing is rough enough that the ship's people are afraid, and she tells them plainly that they will come to no harm. She lands in Norfolk having been away nearly two years, and goes home to Lynn, where the town has not forgotten what she was before she left.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 44
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The Zeeland packet route between Middelburg and the East Anglian ports

stops.name: Bristol, waiting six weeks for a ship to Spain
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no month, and the wait is described as some weeks
stops.campa: She comes to Bristol to sail for Compostela and finds every ship arrested for the king's use in the French war. Six weeks she waits, and the crying takes her in the streets and at the sacrament, and the townspeople say she is possessed, or a fraud, or a Lollard who eats no meat. Some come to her for counsel anyway. A man who mocked her openly on the road repents and asks her forgiveness. She has no money for the passage until a stranger gives it to her, and she goes aboard on the day the ships are released.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 45
suggested_refs: St Mary Redcliffe, Bristol, and the arrested pilgrim shipping of 1417

stops.name: Henbury, examined by the Bishop of Worcester's men
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Book gives no month
stops.campa: Thomas Peverel, Bishop of Worcester, lies sick at Henbury outside Bristol, and sends for her. His household meet her first, young men in slashed and jagged clothes, and she tells them to their faces that they are the devil's men and will burn for their pride unless they amend. The bishop hears of it and receives her anyway. He knew her father, he says, a worshipful man of Lynn. He gives her his blessing, keeps her at his table until she sails, and adds his name to the list of bishops who examined her and found nothing.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 45
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: Thomas Peverel, Bishop of Worcester 1407-1419, and his manor at Henbury

stops.name: Santiago de Compostela, seven days at sea and fourteen at the shrine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the journey; the sailing dates are not preserved, and the round trip is placed by scholars within 1417 to 1418
stops.campa: The crossing takes seven days. She is fourteen days at the shrine of Saint James and the Book, which spends chapters on a quarrel at a dinner table, says almost nothing of what she saw there: only that she had great cheer both bodily and ghostly, and high devotion, and much weeping. Then seven days back to Bristol. Of all her journeys this is the one she keeps to herself, a vow made and a vow paid, with the detail left out that she gives so freely everywhere else.
stops.quote: And so sche toke hir schip in the name of Jhesu and seylyd forth wyth hir felaschip ... thei comyn to Seynt Jamys on the sevenyth day.
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 45 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 45
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The cathedral of Santiago de Compostela and the English sea route from Bristol

stops.name: Hailes Abbey, the relic of the Holy Blood
stops.date_confidence: attested that she went; the sources disagree on the year, the geography placing it in 1417 and the chronology in 1418, and the disagreement is left standing
stops.campa: Back from Spain she goes inland to the Cistercian house at Hailes, under the Cotswold edge, where a phial said to hold the blood of Christ has drawn pilgrims for a century and a half. She is shown the relic, and confesses, and the crying and roaring take her there so that the monks swear great oaths at her and she rebukes them for it. She is on the road home through the middle of England, weeping at every shrine she passes, and the country is at that moment hunting Lollards in earnest.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 46
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The Holy Blood of Hailes, destroyed at the Dissolution; the abbey ruins survive near Winchcombe

stops.name: Leicester, three weeks in the mayor's keeping
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no month, and the detention is described as about three weeks
stops.campa: In a church at Leicester she sees a crucifix and the fire of love kindles so that she breaks out crying, and the mayor has her brought before him. He calls her a false strumpet, a false Lollard and a false deceiver of the people, and asks her where she comes from and whose daughter she is. She tells him: Lynn, and John Brunham's daughter, who was mayor of that town five times. He holds her three weeks anyway. Before the abbot and his assessors she answers the question they all ask, on the sacrament of the altar, and answers it orthodox.
stops.quote: what man hath takyn the ordyr of presthode ... I beleve that it is hys very flesch and hys blood
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 48 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I chs. 46-48
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The Leicester examination before the abbot, the mayor, and the Dean of Leicester

stops.name: York Minster, before the Archbishop
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the archbishop is traditionally identified as Henry Bowet, and the Book does not name him
stops.campa: Brought into the chapter house at York, she is set on a stool before the archbishop and his clerks, and the crowd outside says she should be burned. He tells her she is a wicked woman; she tells him he is a wicked man. He puts the articles of the faith to her and she answers them all, so that the clerks say she knows them well. Then he demands she swear to leave off teaching in his diocese, since a woman may not preach, and she answers that she uses only conversation and good words. He lets her go, and pays a man to lead her out of Yorkshire.
stops.quote: I am non heretyke, ne ye schal non preve me.
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 52 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I chs. 51-52
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The chapter house of York Minster, setting of the fullest of her recorded examinations

stops.name: Beverley Minster, the crowd that calls for burning
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no month
stops.campa: The Duke of Bedford's men take her on the road and bring her to Beverley, where she is shut in a chamber and the women of the town lean from the windows across the street to bring her wine and spices and weep for her. The crowd in the street below says she should be burned, and the friar who accuses her has been preaching against her for months. She is examined again, and again there is nothing to hold her on. Patience, she tells them at York and at Beverley both, is worth more than working miracles.
stops.quote: for pacyens is more worthy than myraclys werkyng
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 51 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 53
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: Beverley Minster and the 1417 Yorkshire heresy sweep following the Oldcastle rising

stops.name: Hessle, arrested at the Humber ferry
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no month
stops.campa: At the Humber crossing at Hessle, waiting for the ferry, she is taken a third time. The men say she is a false Lollard woman and shall be burned, and they hale her back toward Beverley calling her names in the road. Leicester, York, Beverley, and now the ferry: four seizures on one journey home, and four times let go. No court in England finds anything to hold in what she says. The crowds go by the noise she makes in church, which no court has been asked to rule on.
stops.quote: Syr, ye schal welyn sum day that ye had wept as sor as I.
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 52 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition)
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk I ch. 54
suggested_refs: The Hessle ferry crossing of the Humber, the last of the 1417 arrests

stops.name: King's Lynn Minster, home to the town that watches her
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Book narrates the following years thematically and supplies almost no dates for the 1420s
stops.campa: She comes home to Lynn and stays. For more than a decade the record thins to almost nothing: a priest who reads to her for seven years, a fire at the Guildhall that she is credited with quenching by prayer, the crying that comes on her in the parish church and empties the pews around her, quarrels with confessors, sickness, and a reputation the town cannot decide about. She and John Kempe live apart by now, still married. The Book keeps no count of the years, and neither does anything else in Lynn.
stops.quote_source: The Book of Margery Kempe, Book I ch. 45 (Lynn Staley, TEAMS edition), cried out during a Corpus Christi procession

segments.name: Prussia, Wilsnack, and the Priest's Pen

stops.name: King's Lynn, the husband and the son buried in one year
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no months, and the two deaths fall close together
stops.campa: John Kempe falls down a stair in his old age and cracks his head, and she is blamed for living apart from him; she takes him back into her house and nurses him through his last years, washing him like a child, and counts the labour a mercy for the delight she once took in his body. He dies. In the same year the eldest son dies too, the merchant who had settled in Danzig and come home with a German wife. Two graves in Lynn in twelve months, and the woman who buries them is nearly sixty.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk II chs. 1-2
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The opening chapters of Book II, on the son's return, his death, and John Kempe's last illness

stops.name: St Mary's, Danzig, the furthest east she goes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no month
stops.campa: Her widowed daughter-in-law is going home to Prussia and does not want company. She goes down to the ship at Ipswich to see her off and, told in her soul to sail with her, boards without a licence, without money, and without leave. The crossing runs before storms and takes them off course to Norway. In Danzig she stays five or six weeks in a great brick city of the Hanse where nobody knows her, understands little of what is said around her, and cannot easily find a ship home. She is about sixty years old.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk II chs. 2-3
suggested_refs: The Hanseatic port of Danzig, trading partner of Lynn and home of her son's household

stops.name: Wilsnack, the bleeding hosts
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no month
stops.campa: She goes overland out of Prussia through country at war, on foot and in carts, to see the Precious Blood at Wilsnack: three hosts found unburnt and bloodied in the ashes of a church fire fifty years before, drawing crowds that men said rivalled Compostela. Her companion is a man who is ashamed of her weeping and abandons her twice on the road. She sees the relic. Then she walks on toward Aachen with strangers, an old woman with no language and no money crossing Germany because she said she would.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk II ch. 5
suggested_refs: The Wunderblutkirche of Bad Wilsnack, its pilgrimage suppressed and the relic destroyed in 1552

stops.name: Aachen, the showing of the great relics
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the Book gives no month, and the Aachen relics were shown at fixed intervals
stops.campa: At Aachen the cathedral shows its relics only every seven years, and the crowds for it fill the town. She waits for the showing among strangers, lodging where she can, and passes a night in a barn with poor women who strip and pick vermin from their clothes in front of her. She sees the relics. Then she attaches herself to a party going west, is left behind, catches them up, and comes to Calais so ill and so poor that the women who take her in wash her and give her a clean smock.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk II chs. 6-7
suggested_refs: The Aachen septennial showing of the great relics, and the pilgrim crowds it drew

stops.name: Syon Abbey, Isleworth, the pardon of Lammas Day
stops.date_confidence: attested to the return leg of the 1433 to 1434 journey; the vaguer dating of 1431 or later confuses the visit with the abbey's move to Isleworth
stops.campa: On the way home she goes to the Bridgettine house at Syon on the Thames for the pardon granted there, among nuns and brothers who keep the strictest rule in England and who read, as she does not, the books of the continental women visionaries. A young man who had scorned her at Lynn finds her there and asks her forgiveness. She receives the pardon, and goes back to Norfolk. It is the last journey of her life and she has been travelling, on and off, for more than twenty years.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Bk II ch. 9
Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: Syon Abbey at Isleworth, the Bridgettine house and its library of women's revelations

stops.name: King's Lynn, the priest begins to write on the twenty-third of July
stops.date_confidence: attested by the manuscript's own internal dating; this is the day the rewriting began, not the day it was finished
stops.campa: The first attempt is already made and already ruined: her son wrote it down in a hand between English and German that nobody can read, and then he died. Priest after priest refuses the work, afraid of what the town says about her. At last one takes it, probably her confessor, and on the twenty-third of July he begins again from the top, reading the dead man's script with her at his elbow, saying what she said before, until the whole of it is set down. She cannot read a word of what he writes.
sources: The Book of Margery Kempe, Proem

stops.name: Trinity Guildhall, King's Lynn, the last line of the record
stops.date_confidence: attested that a Margery Kempe is admitted in this year; the identification with the author is generally accepted but not proven
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of April the priest begins the second book, the Prussian journey set down after the fact. In the same year the Trinity Guild of Lynn admits a member named Margery Kempe, the great fraternity of the town her father served as mayor. It is almost certainly her, and it is the last line the documents hold. No burial, no will, no year of death, no grave. The record stops there. The woman who could not read leaves behind the first book in English in which anyone tells their own life.
sources: Trinity Guild of Lynn admission records, cited via Wikipedia and Windeatt's introduction
The Book of Margery Kempe, Book II internal dating
suggested_refs: The Trinity Guildhall on Saturday Market Place, King's Lynn, and the guild's admission rolls for 1438

stops.name: Southgate House, Chesterfield, the manuscript identified
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of identification; the exact circumstances of the finding are not recorded in any source consulted
stops.campa: For nearly five hundred years the only copy sits on a shelf in a Derbyshire house belonging to the Butler-Bowdon family, read by nobody, catalogued as nothing. Albert Van de Put of the Victoria and Albert Museum borrows it and shows it to Hope Emily Allen, an American scholar of English mystical writing, and she knows what it is. The story that it turned up in a cupboard among ping-pong bats is told everywhere and confirmed nowhere. In 1934 a book nobody had read for five hundred years acquires a name and a date and an author.
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Book of Margery Kempe'
Wikipedia, 'Hope Emily Allen'
suggested_refs: The Butler-Bowdon library at Southgate House, Chesterfield, and the four annotating hands in the manuscript

stops.name: Oxford, the Early English Text Society edition
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Two years after the identification, Colonel Butler-Bowdon publishes a modernized version of his own with an introduction by R. W. Chambers, and the reading public meets her first in that softened spelling. The scholarly text follows in 1940, edited by Sanford Brown Meech with a prefatory note by Hope Emily Allen, Early English Text Society, Original Series 212. Allen was to have written a second volume of commentary and never finished it. The Middle English is on the page at last, unsmoothed, the town abbreviated to a single letter N.
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Book of Margery Kempe'
Open Library record for W. Butler-Bowdon, 'The Book of Margery Kempe 1436' (Jonathan Cape, 1936)
suggested_refs: EETS Original Series 212 (1940), the first scholarly edition of the Middle English text

stops.name: London, Sotheby's and the British Library
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1980; the day is not recorded in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In June 1980 Captain Maurice Butler-Bowdon puts the manuscript up at Sotheby's and the British Library buys it. It goes into the collection as Additional MS 61823, one small volume in a red-inked hand with three other hands annotating in the margins, one of them a Carthusian reader marking the passages that moved him. Translations follow it out into the world: Windeatt in 1985, Staley in 2001, Bale in 2015. The book that could not find a scribe in Lynn can now be ordered up by anyone with a reader's card.
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Book of Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: British Library Additional MS 61823, the unique manuscript of the Book

stops.name: Oroso, Galicia, the statue on the medieval bridge
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Six hundred years after she came down this road weeping, Galicia sets up a figure of her at the entrance of a medieval bridge at Oroso, on the last stage of the way into Compostela. The pilgrims who pass it are walking the road she reached by seven days at sea and a stranger's charity, and about which she afterwards said almost nothing: fourteen days at the shrine, great cheer bodily and ghostly, and not one line of description. She stands now as a waymark on the road she declined to describe, in a country whose language she never learned, and the walkers who pass her know her name.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
suggested_refs: The Kempe statue at the medieval bridge in Oroso, on the Camino into Santiago

stops.name: King's Lynn Minster, A Woman in Motion
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: In the church where she was christened, married, and thrown out of the pews for the noise she made, a sculpture of her in pilgrim dress is set up in 2023 and called A Woman in Motion. A bench in the Saturday Market Place has carried her name since 2018; a learned society has carried it since the same year. The bench was unveiled by the mayor of Lynn, holding the office her father held five times. The town that called her a false strumpet, a false Lollard and a false deceiver of the people keeps her now as its own.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Margery Kempe'
